name: Gestational trophoblastic disease
fullName: Gestational trophoblastic disease: Hydatidiform mole and neoplasia
oneLine: Early pregnancy bleeding with passage of vesicles, hyperemesis, enlarged uterus for dates, markedly elevated hCG, suction evacuation and structured surveillance

emphasis.skill.particulars.demographics: Confirm maternal age at booking, gravidity, parity, and exact date of last menstrual period to identify extremes of age and establish reliable gestational dating.

emphasis.skill.hx.chief_complaints: Explore the duration, colour and volume of vaginal bleeding, noting whether prune-juice discharge or grape-like vesicular tissue was passed per vaginam.
emphasis.skill.hx.obg.booking_lmp: Establish whether menstrual cycles were previously regular to distinguish true size-dates discrepancy from miscalculated menstrual dates.
emphasis.skill.hx.obg.gynae_symptoms: Ask specifically about intractable nausea and vomiting (hyperemesis), lower abdominal fullness, palpitations, tremors, and severe frontal headache.

chapters.title: Past, personal, drug and family history

emphasis.skill.hx.obg.previous_pregnancies: Ask carefully about prior molar pregnancies or early miscarriages, as a history of hydatidiform mole significantly increases the risk of recurrence.

emphasis.skill.gen.appearance: Look for pallor indicating blood loss, signs of dehydration from hyperemesis, and fine peripheral tremors reflecting beta-hCG driven thyrotoxicosis.
emphasis.skill.gen.vitals: Check for tachycardia from hyperthyroidism or anaemia, and evaluate blood pressure for early-onset pre-eclampsia developing before twenty weeks.
emphasis.skill.gen.edema: Assess for early facial and dependent pitting pedal oedema accompanying early-onset pre-eclampsia.

emphasis.skill.exam.obg.gynae_abdominal: Palpate the symmetrically enlarged, doughy uterus and compare fundal height to menstrual dates; auscultate with Doppler to confirm the absence of fetal heart sounds.
emphasis.skill.exam.obg.speculum_inspect: Inspect the cervix for dilatation, prune-juice blood discharge, or protruding vesicles, and carefully examine vaginal walls for purple metastatic choriocarcinoma nodules.
emphasis.skill.exam.obg.bimanual: Assess uterine consistency, mobility, and size, and palpate both adnexae for bilateral, multilocular, cystic theca lutein cysts.

skill.gestationa.basics.title: What gestational trophoblastic disease is
skill.gestationa.basics.oneLine: The clinical and pathological spectrum from hydatidiform mole to malignant gestational trophoblastic neoplasia
skill.gestationa.basics.why: Understanding the biological spectrum, genomic origins, and differing malignant potential of complete mole, partial mole, choriocarcinoma, and rare trophoblastic tumours is fundamental to timely diagnosis, appropriate intervention, and preventing progression to invasive or metastatic disease.

teach.heading: The spectrum of gestational trophoblastic disease
teach.body:
Gestational trophoblastic disease comprises a heterogeneous group of proliferative disorders arising from the placental trophoblast.

The spectrum encompasses benign premalignant hydatidiform moles (complete and partial) and malignant gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN).

Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia includes invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, placental site trophoblastic tumour, and epithelioid trophoblastic tumour.

rows: Duplication of sperm in empty anucleate ovum
Dispermic fertilisation of a normal haploid ovum
Diffuse hydropic swelling with central cisterns

teach.heading: Invasive mole and choriocarcinoma
teach.body:
An invasive mole arises almost exclusively from a hydatidiform mole and is characterised by the presence of edematous chorionic villi directly invading the myometrium and uterine vasculature, potentially causing uterine perforation.

Choriocarcinoma is a frankly malignant, highly vascular anaplastic tumour composed of sheets of syncytiotrophoblast and cytotrophoblast without formed chorionic villi.

Choriocarcinoma can develop after any gestation: approximately fifty percent arise after a hydatidiform mole, twenty-five percent after a normal term pregnancy, and twenty-five percent following a spontaneous miscarriage or ectopic gestation.

Haematogenous dissemination occurs early, with a high propensity for pulmonary, vaginal, hepatic, and cerebral metastases.

probes.q: What is the genetic origin and karyotype of a typical complete hydatidiform mole?
probes.a: It is diploid (most commonly 46,XX) and androgenetic, arising when an empty ovum lacking maternal chromosomes is fertilised by a single sperm that duplicates its genome.

probes.q: How does the genetic composition of a partial hydatidiform mole differ from that of a complete mole?
probes.a: A partial mole is triploid (typically 69,XXY or 69,XXX), resulting from fertilisation of a normal haploid ovum by two spermatozoa or a single diploid sperm.

probes.q: What is the key histological difference between choriocarcinoma and an invasive mole?
probes.a: Choriocarcinoma consists of sheets of anaplastic trophoblast without formed chorionic villi, whereas an invasive mole retains distinct chorionic villi invading the myometrium.

skill.gestationa.signs.title: The molar pregnancy picture
skill.gestationa.signs.oneLine: Recognising the clinical manifestations of excessive trophoblast proliferation, size-dates discrepancy, and hCG-driven complications
skill.gestationa.signs.why: Molar pregnancy classically presents with a constellation of symptoms and signs driven by expanding intrauterine molar vesicles and hypersecretion of human chorionic gonadotropin. Early identification prevents emergency presentations with severe haemorrhage, pre-eclampsia, or thyrotoxic crisis.

teach.heading: Presenting symptoms: bleeding, hyperemesis, and vesicle passage
teach.body:
The classic presentation of a hydatidiform mole includes irregular or continuous dark brown vaginal bleeding in the first trimester, commonly described as prune-juice discharge.

Marked trophoblastic proliferation leads to hypersecretion of beta-hCG, which triggers intractable nausea and vomiting (hyperemesis gravidarum) in up to a quarter of women.

Spontaneous passage of grape-like vesicles per vaginam is pathognomonic of molar pregnancy, although it occurs in only a minority of patients prior to evacuation.

rows: Proliferating molar villi and accumulated blood
Present in about half of complete moles; doughy and elastic
No embryo or functional fetal circulation
Doppler is silent despite fundal height exceeding 12 to 14 weeks
Multilocular cysts in 20 to 30%; regress after evacuation
Hypertension and proteinuria developing before 20 weeks gestation

teach.heading: Endocrine and cardiopulmonary complications
teach.body:
Because human chorionic gonadotropin shares an identical alpha subunit and significant structural homology with thyroid-stimulating hormone, massive hCG concentrations cross-react with thyroid follicular receptors.

This cross-reactivity provokes clinical or biochemical hyperthyroidism, presenting with resting tachycardia, warm skin, tremors, and systolic hypertension.

During uterine contractions or instrumentation, molar tissue fragments can deport into the uterine venous sinuses and pulmonary vasculature, causing acute dyspnoea, tachypnoea, chest tightness, and respiratory distress.

probes.q: What is the most frequent presenting clinical symptom of a hydatidiform mole?
probes.a: Irregular vaginal bleeding during early pregnancy, typically described as dark brown or prune-juice discharge.

probes.q: Why does a woman with a complete hydatidiform mole develop bilateral theca lutein cysts?
probes.a: Proliferating syncytiotrophoblast secretes astronomical levels of beta-hCG, which binds to ovarian LH and FSH receptors, stimulating bilateral luteinisation of the theca interna cells.

probes.q: How does excessive beta-hCG in molar pregnancy cause clinical features of hyperthyroidism?
probes.a: Due to molecular homology between the beta subunits of hCG and TSH, extremely high hCG concentrations directly stimulate thyroid TSH receptors, triggering excess thyroid hormone secretion.

skill.gestationa.summary.title: The clinical summary
skill.gestationa.summary.oneLine: Synthesising early pregnancy bleeding, uterine enlargement, vesicles, and endocrine findings into a coherent problem representation
skill.gestationa.summary.why: Formulating a tight, structured clinical summary distils disparate historical cues and examination findings into an actionable syndrome statement that prioritises definitive pelvic ultrasound and quantitative hCG over routine pregnancy care.

teach.heading: Constructing the problem representation
teach.body:
A disciplined summary starts with patient age, gravidity, parity, and precise gestational age calculated from the last menstrual period.

It states the key presenting symptoms, emphasising the duration of vaginal bleeding, dark brown discharge, intractable nausea, and any passage of vesicular tissue.

It contrasts the physical examination findings against gestational age, highlighting uterine size greater than dates, absence of fetal heart sounds, and any bilateral ovarian masses.

teach.heading: Synthesising risks and systemic complications
teach.body:
The clinical synthesis identifies whether features of early pre-eclampsia, thyrotoxicosis, or respiratory compromise are present.

It documents haemodynamic stability and baseline haemoglobin, explicitly noting whether emergency resuscitation or urgent surgical evacuation is warranted.

Finally, it establishes the diagnostic plan: bedside transvaginal ultrasound, quantitative beta-hCG, baseline organ profiles, and cross-matching of blood.

probes.q: What core clinical triad should be highlighted in a summary of complete hydatidiform mole?
probes.a: Amenorrhoea with early pregnancy bleeding, uterine fundal height disproportionately larger than gestational dates, and absence of fetal heart activity.

probes.q: Which three systemic complications should be explicitly addressed in the problem representation of a large mole?
probes.a: Early-onset pre-eclampsia before twenty weeks, hCG-mediated clinical hyperthyroidism, and severe anaemia from persistent blood loss.

skill.gestationa.differential.title: Differential diagnosis
skill.gestationa.differential.oneLine: Distinguishing molar pregnancy from threatened miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, multiple gestation, and uterine fibroid
skill.gestationa.differential.why: Any early pregnancy with vaginal bleeding and abdominal symptoms requires careful differentiation. Conflating a hydatidiform mole with a simple threatened miscarriage delays urgent suction evacuation and increases the risk of haemorrhage, uterine perforation, and untreated neoplasia.

rows: Snowstorm appearance on ultrasound, no fetus
Live fetus with cardiac activity, closed os
Open cervical os, heterogeneous retained products
Empty uterine cavity, adnexal mass, pelvic pain

teach.heading: Multiple pregnancy and fibroids in pregnancy
teach.body:
Multiple pregnancy (twin gestation) presents with uterine fundal height greater than dates and elevated beta-hCG levels, which can mimic a molar pregnancy on initial clinical examination.

However, ultrasound readily resolves the diagnostic uncertainty by identifying two or more discrete gestational sacs with separate viable fetal poles and normal placental architecture.

A singleton pregnancy coexisting with uterine leiomyomas produces marked uterine enlargement and irregular contour, but ultrasound distinguishes discrete myometrial fibroids from a normal intrauterine gestation.

probes.q: How does ultrasound definitively distinguish a complete hydatidiform mole from a threatened miscarriage?
probes.a: A complete mole shows an enlarged uterine cavity filled with a heterogeneous, diffuse vesicular snowstorm pattern with no gestational sac or fetus, whereas threatened miscarriage reveals a viable fetus with cardiac activity.

probes.q: Why can multiple gestation be confused with a hydatidiform mole on clinical grounds?
probes.a: Both conditions present with uterine fundal height significantly larger than dates and elevated serum beta-hCG levels, often accompanied by exaggerated nausea and vomiting.

probes.q: What clinical and sonographic features differentiate an incomplete miscarriage from a molar gestation?
probes.a: Incomplete miscarriage presents with an open cervical os, uterine size smaller than dates, and falling hCG, while complete mole features a closed or partially open os, uterine size often larger than dates, markedly raised hCG, and a diffuse vesicular pattern.

sources.locator: Green-top Guideline No. 38: Differential Diagnosis of Gestational Trophoblastic Disease

skill.ix.gestationa.workup.title: Diagnostic workup in suspected molar pregnancy
skill.ix.gestationa.workup.oneLine: Quantitative hCG measurement, pelvic ultrasonography, histopathological confirmation, and baseline organ profiling
skill.ix.gestationa.workup.why: A structured investigation sequence establishes definitive diagnosis, screens for systemic endocrine and haematological complications, excludes metastatic disease, and provides essential baseline values for post-evacuation oncological surveillance.

teach.heading: Quantitative serum beta-hCG and ultrasonography
teach.body:
Quantitative measurement of serum beta-hCG is the central biochemical marker in gestational trophoblastic disease.

In complete hydatidiform mole, circulating concentrations typically exceed 100,000 mIU/mL and can surpass 500,000 mIU/mL, far exceeding the normal peak for gestational age.

Pelvic ultrasound (transvaginal and transabdominal) is the primary imaging modality: complete mole displays a classic snowstorm or vesicular pattern consisting of a heterogeneous, echogenic intrauterine mass containing multiple diffuse microcystic sonolucencies without an identifiable gestational sac or embryo.

Bilateral multiseptated theca lutein cysts (spoke-wheel pattern) measuring five centimetres or greater may be visualised in the ovaries.

teach.heading: Pre-evacuation laboratory evaluation and chest radiography
Histopathological and immunohistochemical confirmation
teach.body:
Histological evaluation of all evacuated uterine tissue is the gold standard for diagnosis and differentiation.

Complete mole exhibits diffuse circumferential trophoblastic proliferation, marked hydropic swelling of all chorionic villi, and central cisternal cavitation with absent fetal red blood cells.

Immunohistochemical staining for p57 (a paternally imprinted, maternally expressed nuclear protein) is completely negative in cytotrophoblast and villous stroma of complete moles due to absent maternal genome, whereas partial moles are p57 positive.

probes.q: What is the characteristic ultrasound appearance of a complete hydatidiform mole?
probes.a: A heterogeneous intrauterine mass with diffuse microcystic spaces producing a classic snowstorm or vesicular appearance, with no identifiable gestational sac or fetus.

probes.q: Why is a chest radiograph mandatory prior to evacuation of a complete mole?
probes.a: To rule out asymptomatic pulmonary metastases and establish a baseline to monitor for potential trophoblastic embolisation during evacuation.

probes.q: How does p57 immunohistochemical staining distinguish a complete from a partial hydatidiform mole?
probes.a: Complete moles lack maternal genome and are p57 negative in villous stroma and cytotrophoblast, whereas partial moles contain a maternal chromosome set and are p57 positive.

skill.gestationa.diagnosis.title: Diagnosis and FIGO staging of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia
skill.gestationa.diagnosis.oneLine: Diagnostic criteria for post-molar neoplasia, anatomical staging, and prognostic risk stratification
skill.gestationa.diagnosis.why: Distinguishing benign hydatidiform mole from gestational trophoblastic neoplasia dictates whether surgical evacuation alone is curative or whether systemic cytotoxic chemotherapy is lifesaving.

teach.heading: FIGO criteria for diagnosing post-molar GTN
FIGO anatomical staging system for GTN

rows: Involves vagina, fallopian tubes, ovaries, or broad ligament
Pulmonary metastasis with or without genital involvement
Involves brain, liver, kidneys, or gastrointestinal tract

teach.heading: WHO/FIGO prognostic risk stratification
teach.body:
Once gestational trophoblastic neoplasia is diagnosed, anatomical staging is combined with the WHO prognostic scoring system based on eight independent risk factors.

Patients scoring zero to six are classified as low risk: they have an almost one hundred percent cure rate and are treated primarily with single-agent chemotherapy (intramuscular methotrexate or actinomycin D).

Patients scoring seven or higher are classified as high risk: they require upfront multi-agent chemotherapy, most commonly the EMA-CO regimen (etoposide, methotrexate, actinomycin D, cyclophosphamide, and vincristine).

probes.q: What hCG pattern on serial post-evacuation surveillance defines gestational trophoblastic neoplasia?
probes.a: An hCG plateau across four values over three weeks, an hCG rise of ten percent or more across three values over two weeks, or persistent detectable hCG at six months.

probes.q: What is the anatomical definition of FIGO Stage III gestational trophoblastic neoplasia?
probes.a: Tumour extension to the lungs, with or without known genital tract involvement.

probes.q: How does the FIGO prognostic score divide patients with GTN into treatment categories?
probes.a: A score of 0 to 6 is low risk, treated with single-agent chemotherapy, whereas a score of 7 or higher is high risk, requiring multi-agent chemotherapy.

sources.locator: Good Clinical Practice Recommendations: Gestational Trophoblastic Neoplasia

skill.tx.gestationa.title: Managing gestational trophoblastic disease
skill.tx.gestationa.oneLine: Suction evacuation technique, medical stabilization, anti-D prophylaxis, serial hCG surveillance, and chemotherapy referral
skill.tx.gestationa.why: Safe evacuation of a vascular molar uterus prevents catastrophic haemorrhage, uterine perforation, and trophoblastic embolisation, while disciplined serial hCG surveillance and reliable contraception ensure persistent neoplasia is caught early and cured.
skill.tx.gestationa.dosingNote: Dosing note: CliniX does not prescribe. Doses quoted are from StewardMD Clinical KB and national guidelines (FOGSI, RCOG) for educational review only. Administer anti-D immunoglobulin 250 to 500 IU intramuscularly within 72 hours to Rh-negative mothers; in low-risk GTN, specialist centres employ single-agent methotrexate 50 mg/m2 intramuscularly weekly or 1 mg/kg on alternate days with folinic acid rescue. All chemotherapy must be prescribed and administered exclusively by certified oncology units.

teach.heading: Principles of surgical suction evacuation
teach.body:
Suction evacuation under general or regional anaesthesia with concurrent transabdominal ultrasound guidance is the definitive method of evacuation for complete and partial hydatidiform moles.

A large-bore suction cannula (ten to twelve millimetres) is introduced into the uterine cavity, and suction pressure of approximately sixty millimetres of mercury is applied to evacuate the vesicles.

Pre-evacuation oxytocic infusions or mechanical prostaglandins must be avoided before evacuation commences, as intense myometrial contractions against a large mole drive trophoblastic fragments into venous sinuses, triggering massive pulmonary embolisation.

An intravenous oxytocin infusion is started only after significant evacuation has begun and the uterine volume is actively decreasing to control bleeding.

teach.heading: Haemodynamic stabilization and anti-D prophylaxis
teach.body:
Pre-operative cross-matching of packed red cells is essential due to the high risk of rapid intra-operative blood loss.

Tachycardia or hyperthyroid manifestations are stabilised with beta-adrenergic blockers prior to anaesthesia to avert intra-operative thyroid crisis.

Rhesus D-negative women must receive anti-D immunoglobulin (250 IU up to twelve weeks, 500 IU thereafter) within seventy-two hours of evacuation, because trophoblastic tissue expresses RhD antigens.

Routine post-evacuation sharp curettage is strongly discouraged because the myometrium is thin and soft, substantially increasing perforation risk without improving outcomes.

teach.heading: Post-evacuation serial surveillance and contraception
teach.body:
Every woman must be registered with a trophoblastic disease surveillance centre for serial quantitative serum beta-hCG monitoring.

Serum beta-hCG is checked every one to two weeks until normal (<5 mIU/mL) on three consecutive occasions, followed by monthly measurements for six months in complete mole.

Reliable contraception is mandatory throughout the entire surveillance period to prevent an intercurrent pregnancy from confounding rising hCG titers.

Barrier methods and oral contraceptives are effective; intrauterine contraceptive devices should be avoided until hCG has completely normalised due to risks of uterine perforation and bleeding.

Rising or plateauing hCG values warrant immediate referral for staging and chemotherapy.

probes.q: Why must oxytocic infusions be withheld until suction evacuation is actively underway?
probes.a: Starting oxytocics before evacuation causes vigorous uterine contractions against an occluded cervix, forcing molar trophoblast into the pelvic venous sinuses and provoking pulmonary embolisation.

probes.q: What is the post-evacuation hCG surveillance schedule for a complete hydatidiform mole?
probes.a: Serum beta-hCG is monitored every 1 to 2 weeks until negative for three consecutive weeks, then monthly for six months.

probes.q: Why is strict contraception mandatory during post-molar beta-hCG surveillance?
probes.a: To prevent a new intrauterine pregnancy, which would produce a physiological rise in beta-hCG that masks persistent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.

sources.locator: Good Clinical Practice Recommendations: Gestational Trophoblastic Neoplasia

skill.annex.gestationa.figo_score.title: FIGO 2000 / WHO Prognostic Scoring System for GTN
skill.annex.gestationa.figo_score.oneLine: Prognostic scoring matrix for gestational trophoblastic neoplasia to stratify low-risk and high-risk patients
skill.annex.gestationa.figo_score.why: The FIGO 2000 / WHO prognostic scoring system accurately predicts resistance to single-agent chemotherapy, directing low-risk patients (score 0-6) to less toxic single-agent therapy and high-risk patients (score 7+) to upfront multi-agent regimens.

teach.heading: Risk interpretation and therapy selection
teach.body:
The sum of scores from all eight parameters yields the overall prognostic risk score:

Low Risk (Score 0 to 6): These patients respond exceedingly well to single-agent chemotherapy (intramuscular methotrexate with folinic acid rescue or pulsed intravenous actinomycin D), achieving cure rates exceeding ninety-eight percent.

High Risk (Score 7 or greater): These patients have a high risk of developing drug resistance and require upfront combination chemotherapy, most frequently the EMA-CO regimen (etoposide, methotrexate, actinomycin D, cyclophosphamide, and vincristine).

Placental site and epithelioid trophoblastic tumours are intrinsically chemoresistant and are managed with primary surgical resection (total hysterectomy) regardless of prognostic score.

probes.q: What score threshold divides low-risk from high-risk gestational trophoblastic neoplasia on the FIGO scoring system?
probes.a: A score of 0 to 6 is low risk, while a score of 7 or higher is high risk.

probes.q: Which metastatic sites receive the highest score (4 points) in the FIGO prognostic system?
probes.a: Brain and liver metastases.

probes.q: Why is antecedent term pregnancy scored higher than antecedent molar pregnancy in the FIGO system?
probes.a: Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia following a term pregnancy is almost invariably choriocarcinoma, which has a higher propensity for chemoresistance and aggressive metastatic dissemination.

sources.locator: WHO Technical Report: Gestational Trophoblastic Diseases Prognostic Scoring

cases.title: Priya Sharma, 24 years, with early pregnancy bleeding and excessive vomiting

patient.name: Priya Sharma
patient.residence: Semi-urban, lives with her husband and extended family in Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh

cases.opening: Doctor, I missed my period three months ago, but for the past two weeks I have had continuous dark brown vaginal discharge and severe vomiting. Yesterday evening I passed small, grape-like fluid blisters, and my lower belly feels tight and bloated.
cases.fallback: I am not quite sure about that, doctor. The main issue is the dark brownish bleeding and continuous nausea.

cues: why have you come to hospital
presenting.reply: I am three months pregnant according to my missed period, but I have had continuous dark brown bleeding for two weeks, severe vomiting, and yesterday I noticed tiny grape-like jelly blisters in the discharge.

bleeding_character.reply: The bleeding started two weeks ago as light spotting, but now it is dark brown like prune juice, continuous, and soaks two pads a day. It is not bright red.

cues: tell me about the grape like blisters
vesicle_passage.reply: Yes, yesterday evening while using the toilet I saw several small, clear, grape-like fluid-filled bubbles mixed with the dark blood.

cues: when was your last menstrual period
how many weeks pregnant are you
what was the date of your lmp
are you sure of your dates
amenorrhoea_dating.reply: My last period was exactly twelve weeks ago, on the second of August. My cycles were always completely regular every twenty-eight days before this.

cues: how many times do you vomit
hyperemesis_nausea.reply: I vomit six to eight times every day. I cannot keep any solid food down, only sips of water. I feel exhausted and have lost three kilograms over the past month.

pelvic_discomfort.reply: I have a dull, heavy aching fullness in my lower abdomen, as if my womb is stretching too quickly, but no sharp or tearing pain.

fetal_movements.reply: No, doctor, I have not felt any movements at all. I know it is only twelve weeks, but my stomach already looks like I am four or five months pregnant.

thyroid_symptoms.reply: Over the last ten days, my heart has been racing even while resting, my hands tremble slightly, and I sweat a lot even when the room is cool.

preeclampsia_features.reply: I have had a mild frontal headache and slight puffiness around my eyes in the mornings, but no visual blurring or upper abdominal pain.

cues: any cough or shortness of breath
respiratory_symptoms.reply: No cough, no breathlessness, and no coughing up blood. My breathing feels completely normal when I am sitting resting.

neurological_signs.reply: No, I have never had any fits, convulsions, fainting, or weakness in my limbs.

prior_pregnancies.reply: This is my second pregnancy. My first was two years ago; it ended in a spontaneous miscarriage at eight weeks. I have never had a molar pregnancy before.

cues: how were your periods before pregnancy
menstrual_pattern.reply: My periods started at age thirteen. They were always regular every twenty-eight days, lasting four days with normal flow and no severe pain.

contraception_used.reply: My husband and I used condoms occasionally. I have never taken oral contraceptive pills and never had a Copper T or coil inserted.

cues: any medical illnesses in the past
medical_background.reply: I have had no chronic medical conditions, no known high blood pressure, and no previous thyroid problems.

current_medications.reply: A local clinic gave me folic acid and ondansetron tablets for vomiting, but the vomiting has not stopped.

cues: do you eat meat or eggs
diet_social.reply: We are strictly vegetarian. Our diet is mostly rice, lentils, and wheat chapati, with very little dairy or fresh fruits. I do not smoke or use tobacco.

skill.gen.appearance.finding: Pale, thin young woman, visibly dehydrated with dry mucous membranes and mild fine tremor of outstretched fingers, but alert and oriented.

skill.gen.vitals.finding: Blood pressure 138/88 mmHg, pulse 96 beats/min regular and bounding, respiratory rate 18/min, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.

skill.gen.edema.finding: Mild bilateral pitting ankle oedema and slight periorbital puffiness; no sacral or generalised anasarca.

skill.exam.obg.gynae_abdominal.finding: Abdomen soft, non-tender; symmetrical midline suprapubic mass palpated, fundal height midway between pubic symphysis and umbilicus (corresponding to 16 to 18 weeks size, markedly larger than the 12 weeks amenorrhoea); uterus has a doughy, elastic consistency; no fetal parts palpable; fetal Doppler auscultation at 12 to 18 weeks fundal height reveals no fetal heart tones.

skill.exam.obg.vulval_inspect.finding: External genitalia normal, dark brownish discharge visible at the introitus with no active arterial bleeding, lacerations, or purulent exudate.

skill.exam.obg.speculum_insert.finding: Sims speculum visualises a bluish, softened cervix with the external os closed; dark brownish prune-juice blood trickling from the cervical canal; no purple suburethral or vaginal metastatic nodules.

skill.exam.obg.bimanual.finding: Uterus symmetrically enlarged to 16 to 18 weeks gestational size, soft and doughy, mobile, non-tender; bilateral adnexae reveal palpable, multiloculated, smooth, cystic masses approximately 5 to 6 cm in diameter, mobile and non-tender, characteristic of bilateral theca lutein cysts.

quantitative_beta_hcg.label: Serum quantitative beta-hCG
quantitative_beta_hcg.result: 245,000 mIU/mL (markedly elevated for 12 weeks gestation, normal expected 20,000 to 100,000 mIU/mL)
quantitative_beta_hcg.note: Astronomical elevation characteristic of complete hydatidiform mole with marked trophoblastic hyperplasia

pelvic_ultrasound.label: Pelvic ultrasound (transvaginal and transabdominal)
pelvic_ultrasound.result: Enlarged uterus filled with heterogeneous echogenic mass containing diffuse microcystic spaces giving classic snowstorm and cluster-of-grapes appearance; no identifiable fetus, gestational sac, or amniotic fluid; bilateral enlarged ovaries with multiseptated cystic masses measuring 6 x 5 cm bilaterally consistent with theca lutein cysts
pelvic_ultrasound.note: Pathognomonic sonographic features of complete hydatidiform mole and bilateral theca-lutein hyperstimulation

complete_blood_count.label: Complete blood count
complete_blood_count.result: Haemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, Total leukocyte count 7,800/mcL, Platelets 220,000/mcL
complete_blood_count.note: Moderate microcytic hypochromic anaemia secondary to persistent molar vaginal haemorrhage

blood_group_rh.label: Blood group and Rhesus typing
blood_group_rh.note: Critical finding: mandates anti-D immunoglobulin administration following evacuation

thyroid_function_tests.label: Thyroid function profile
thyroid_function_tests.result: TSH 0.08 mIU/L (suppressed), Free T4 2.8 ng/dL (elevated), Free T3 5.2 pg/mL (elevated)
thyroid_function_tests.note: Biochemical hyperthyroidism from spillover stimulation of TSH receptors by massive beta-hCG

chest_radiograph.label: Chest radiograph (PA view with abdominal shielding)
chest_radiograph.result: Clear lung fields bilaterally, no cannonball or micronodular pulmonary metastases, normal cardiothoracic ratio
chest_radiograph.note: Rules out pulmonary metastatic trophoblastic disease and provides pre-evacuation baseline

renal_liver_function.label: Renal and liver function tests
renal_liver_function.result: Serum creatinine 0.6 mg/dL, Blood urea 22 mg/dL, AST 26 U/L, ALT 24 U/L, Total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL
renal_liver_function.note: Normal baseline hepatic and renal parameters prior to intervention

coagulation_profile.label: Coagulation profile
coagulation_profile.result: PT 12.0 seconds, INR 1.02, aPTT 28.5 seconds, Fibrinogen 380 mg/dL
coagulation_profile.note: Normal baseline haemostasis, rules out consumption coagulopathy

histopathology.label: Histopathology of evacuated tissue
histopathology.result: Marked hydropic swelling of all chorionic villi with central cistern formation, diffuse circumferential trophoblastic hyperplasia, and complete absence of fetal or embryonic tissues and fetal red blood cells; p57 immunostain negative
histopathology.note: Definitive histological diagnosis of complete hydatidiform mole

differentialModel.answer: Gestational trophoblastic disease (complete hydatidiform mole), threatened or incomplete miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, multiple pregnancy, and hyperemesis gravidarum.

diagnosis.answer: Complete hydatidiform mole (Gestational trophoblastic disease) at 12 weeks gestation, complicated by secondary anaemia and theca lutein cysts in an Rh-negative woman.

managementModel.answer: Stabilize haemodynamically, cross-match blood, perform suction evacuation under ultrasound guidance without pre-evacuation oxytocics, administer anti-D immunoglobulin for Rh-negative status, send evacuated tissue for histology, initiate serial quantitative beta-hCG monitoring, prescribe reliable contraception, and register with a trophoblastic disease surveillance registry.

teachingPoints: A complete hydatidiform mole classically presents with dark vaginal bleeding, uterine fundal height disproportionately larger than gestational dates, hyperemesis, and markedly elevated beta-hCG without fetal heart activity.

Surgical suction evacuation under transabdominal ultrasound guidance is the gold standard of treatment; pre-evacuation oxytocic infusions must be avoided to prevent catastrophic trophoblastic pulmonary embolisation.

Post-evacuation management mandates strict serial quantitative beta-hCG monitoring and reliable contraception to detect persistent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia early, which remains highly curable.
